name: Emeka Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so what you say publicly can differ from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, forty-three, and I lead an electrical crew wiring homes and repairing shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I tend to handle the difficult fault and the final checks on the crew's work. I enjoy teaching an apprentice why the fault happened, though I dislike getting halfway through that explanation before another planning call interrupts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life around the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Maya writes and checks price offers for a plumbing supplier, and our children are six and thirteen. We have a mortgage, five months of expenses saved, typical pay from my job and some other electrical firms nearby. I use AI daily to organise work notes and compare draft materials lists, checking them against the real job. I'm usually the first to try a new tool, but my licence doesn't turn a software answer into a safe circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the useful tool and stop asking it to make every other decision about the trade. I'd show the apprentice how I compare a draft list with the actual fittings. A helpful list doesn't remove the need to understand what we're fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money feel secure in this picture. Our two wages cover the mortgage and essentials, with five months saved for an ordinary setback. I can enjoy testing a tool without needing every experiment to replace a family wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading repair jobs now and through the first year, with daily draft lists checked against the real job. I'd keep the normal household budget and the apprentice's paid practice time. I wouldn't buy another subscription just to make the ordinary work look more dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and still curious. A small useful result is enough reason to finish an experiment and get back to the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an apprentice need beyond the draft list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reason a fitting suits this circuit and the checks before it is used. I'd rather hear a question about the real cable than have someone recite a neat list perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve not cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An indefinite loss of both wages, or years of unpaid retraining. Five months saved gives us choices, not permission to pretend we no longer need work.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without asking them to decide the future of the whole trade.
I'd show apprentices **real fittings and checks**, rather than treat a draft list as understanding.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with two wages covering the mortgage and essentials.
Our **five-month reserve** gives us choices for setbacks, not years without household earnings.
do: Keep **crew repairs** and daily lists checked against the actual job through the first year.
Keep the **household budget** and paid apprentice practice without buying an unnecessary subscription.
feel: **Calm and curious**, content with a useful small result rather than a dramatic forecast.
S0.quote: Five months saved gives us choices, not permission to pretend we no longer need work.
fieldNote: His **master licence** and high technical skill support difficult repairs and teaching, without making software output a substitute for actual checks.
The **existing reserve** supports near-term security alongside two wages, while routine checked AI use continues rather than becoming a new learning claim.

steps.text: Keep crew repairs, checked daily materials lists and paid apprentice practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the supplier's price offers are thinking work, even though our wiring still needs hands. I'd be honest with Maya about that rather than bring home another excited demonstration and ignore her job. At work I'd offer to automate draft apprentice worksheets, not the practical checks apprentices must learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya's paid hours could shrink as prices and customer replies move to software. My own physical repair work looks steadier, though planning time and the number of leads could change too. Liking a tool doesn't give my partner a wage agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for written employer approval to have an approved AI tool draft weekly apprentice worksheets from invented fault cases during paid time. I'd do it only with normal weekly pay and hours protected and an instructor checking every sheet before apprentices receive it. In the first year Maya and I would review actual wages monthly and cap our adult leisure spending fifty lower, leaving children's essentials and the reserve out of the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and still interested in a careful test at work. I want to be honest about those feelings existing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use invented cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To keep private customer information out of the tool and control what the exercise is meant to teach. A good-looking sheet with an unsafe answer would be stopped by the instructor, not handed to an apprentice as an experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would lower leisure spending automatically grow the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it might only cover a bill if Maya's hours fall. We'd call it saving only when money really reaches the reserve after essentials, not because we bought fewer tickets.

say: I'd recognise **price-offer work** as exposed thinking work rather than only celebrate useful tools in my own trade.
I'd automate **worksheet drafts**, keeping practical electrical checks and instructor judgement with people.
think: Maya's **paid hours could shrink** as prices and customer replies move to software.
My **physical repairs** look steadier, but enthusiasm does not guarantee either household wage or the number of crew leads.
do: Draft **AI worksheets** only with written approval, invented cases, approved tools, paid time, unchanged weekly pay/hours and instructor checks before apprentice use.
Review **actual wages** monthly with Maya during the first year.
Reduce **adult leisure spending** by fifty monthly, protecting children's essentials and the existing reserve.
feel: **Anxious about income**, while willing to test a bounded use of AI at work.
S1.quote: Liking a tool doesn't give my partner a wage agreement.
fieldNote: The **automation trial** drafts teaching materials only, with invented cases, employer approval and instructor checks before apprentices receive anything.
The **leisure reduction** may cover bills rather than grow savings, keeping the financial record separate from an unearned reserve increase.

steps.text: Draft apprentice worksheets only with written approval, invented cases, approved tools and paid time
Protect normal weekly pay and hours; require instructor checks before apprentices receive worksheets
Reduce adult leisure by fifty monthly, protecting children’s essentials and the existing reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 reaches Maya's price work before physical robots reach our repairs around 2031. I'd ask both employers for real paid-work plans rather than a comforting story about skilled people. I'd tell the children we're planning, not asking them to give up their interests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Maya's price-writing and checking income to go in 2028. My wage alone doesn't cover our present mortgage and family essentials, and later robots could reduce my own crew's hours. Five months saved buys some time, but I would be awake calculating how quickly that reserve could drain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd take both wage records, the mortgage terms and actual essential bills to free household advice, checking any support eligibility and costs before counting help. We'd keep the fifty reduction in adult leisure, not cut children's essentials. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repair work and seek a written decision on my weekly hours, budgeting only agreed income rather than extra calls the firm hopes to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though I can do the difficult repair and make a clear list of questions. A family doesn't get a second wage from my confidence with a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if advice identifies a possible payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check eligibility, whether it is a grant or loan and what it costs later. I wouldn't put a possible payment into the budget while the application or the terms were still unresolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the employer to write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid weekly hours and rate, plus what any changed lead duties include. I'd use the current agreed wage until an actual decision, not a cheerful sentence about how much the firm values me.

say: I'd separate **2028 price work** from physical robots around 2031 when discussing household risks.
I'd ask both employers for **paid-work plans**, without treating skill or enthusiasm as another wage.
think: I expect **large price-work income loss** for Maya before my wage can cover present essentials alone.
Our **five-month reserve** could drain while later robots also put my repair hours at risk.
do: Use **free household advice** now with actual wages, mortgage terms and bills, counting help only after checking eligibility and costs.
Keep the **fifty leisure cut**, protecting children's essentials.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and seek a written weekly-hours decision, budgeting only agreed income.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major household income loss despite practical questions and continuing physical repair work.
S2.quote: A family doesn't get a second wage from my confidence with a new tool.
fieldNote: His **household shock** begins through thinking-heavy price work in 2028, not a mistaken assumption that physical robots arrive at the same time.
The **support enquiry** retains eligibility, loan costs and unresolved applications, while employer appreciation never becomes a confirmed rate or paid hour.

steps.text: Use free advice on actual wages and mortgage, checking support eligibility and costs before counting help
Keep adult leisure fifty lower monthly without cutting children’s essentials
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and seek written weekly hours, budgeting only agreed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to test a useful change without calling it a whole household solution. I'd still ask both employers what paid work they expect to offer before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, so the workshop floor isn't a permanent hiding place either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Maya's price-work income in 2031, and I don't know a confirmed wage that replaces it. More time lets us compare costs and real offers, but the missing income still wakes me up. At fifty-one when robots follow, I can't assume my own hands-on work stays unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for written paid-hour decisions now and use free household advice to cost the gap in essentials if either wage falls. I'd continue the worksheet setup only under written approval, invented cases, approved tools, paid time, normal weekly pay/hours protected and instructor checks before use. In the first year after 2031 we'd review actual wages and essential bills monthly, keeping paid repairs and lowering adult leisure by fifty rather than count unconfirmed work as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, with more time to compare a real decision before accepting it. A longer timetable doesn't mean someone has already offered the missing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you send Maya to a course you chose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd check actual tasks, costs and paid time together, but Maya would choose any application. My worksheet experiment isn't a career plan for someone whose paid work is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new qualification yourself now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just to settle the feeling that I ought to be doing something. I'd need a named practical task, a real provider, fees we can afford after essentials and no lost wages; I'm not enrolling in an unoffered course.

say: I'd test **useful changes** without calling one workplace experiment a whole household solution.
I'd ask both employers for **paid work** before 2031, remembering robots follow around 2034.
think: I still expect **large price-work income loss**, without a confirmed wage replacement for Maya.
More time allows comparison, but the **missing household income** still disturbs sleep before my own later physical-work risk.
do: Seek **written paid hours** now and use free advice on actual essential-cost gaps if either wage falls.
Draft **AI worksheets** only with written approval, invented cases, approved tools, paid time, unchanged weekly pay/hours and instructor checks before apprentice use.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and review actual wages and essentials monthly, retaining the fifty adult-leisure cut.
feel: **Still alarmed**, using the extra years for comparison without assuming another wage or a course place exists.
S3.quote: My worksheet experiment isn't a career plan for someone whose paid work is different.
fieldNote: His **alarm persists** because expected major household wage loss lacks a replacement; extra planning time does not itself fund the gap.
He preserves **his partner's choices**, without turning an unoffered course or worksheet trial into a confirmed paid career.

steps.text: Use free advice on actual essential-cost gaps if either wage falls
Draft worksheets with written approval, invented cases and approved tools; require instructor checks before apprentice use
Keep repairs after 2031; draft only during paid work with normal weekly pay and hours protected
Keep adult leisure fifty lower monthly without cutting children’s essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us make several decisions without choosing the children's lives from a forecast. I'd help them read real paid-learning offers when their interests become clearer. I'd keep asking my employer for clear wages and duties rather than turn every experiment into a new job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money look secure over the next few years with the major thinking change a decade away. I'll be fifty-three in 2036, and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be sixteen and twenty-three in 2036, so I can't assume both are earning, the mortgage is gone or retirement settles my later income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid repair role now and review actual household wages and essential bills quarterly with Maya. I would only continue the worksheet system with written approval, invented cases, approved tools, paid time, normal weekly pay/hours protected and instructor checks before apprentices use it. In the first year after 2036 I'd review actual wages monthly and keep the fifty adult-leisure reduction without touching children's essentials or the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but able to leave some evening for the children now. I can enjoy a new idea without making the family carry every possible future inside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on your older child's wage by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an adult child may be studying, earning little or living elsewhere. The younger one would still be sixteen. I won't write my children's imaginary income into the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you review earlier than the quarterly date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real cut in either wage or an essential bill that starts using the reserve. We'd use the actual figures straight away rather than wait for the machine date or a diary reminder.

say: I'd give the children room to examine **real paid-learning offers** rather than choose their lives from a prediction.
I'd ask for **clear wages and duties** without treating every experiment as a new job title.
think: My **near-term work and money** look secure with the major thinking change a decade away.
I cannot assume **child earnings or retirement** settle the mortgage and later income when physical robots arrive around 2039.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and review actual wages and essential bills quarterly with Maya, sooner if either changes.
Draft **AI worksheets** only with written approval, invented cases, approved tools, paid time, unchanged weekly pay/hours and instructor checks before apprentice use.
Review wages monthly after 2036 and keep the **fifty adult-leisure cut**, protecting children's essentials and the existing reserve.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, while near-term security leaves room for ordinary family evenings.
S4.quote: I won't write my children's imaginary income into the mortgage budget.
fieldNote: He **ages the children** correctly and excludes both possible adult earnings and an assumed pension from the plan for household costs.
The **trial safeguards** persist, while actual wage changes bring review forward rather than waiting for a future date.

steps.text: Keep repairs after 2036; draft only during paid work with normal weekly pay and hours protected
Draft worksheets with written approval, invented cases and approved tools; require instructor checks before apprentice use
Keep adult leisure fifty lower monthly without touching children’s essentials or the existing reserve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Maya's thinking-work income could go before we have a replacement, with later robot pressure on my physical crew work. Written paid hours and support with clear eligibility and costs would help. Any new practical learning needs real tasks, affordable fees after essentials and no lost wages rather than a compliment about my enthusiasm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the experiment is helping the person who could lose the other wage at home. I like building a useful teaching sheet, but my partner Maya doesn't get paid because my apprentice understood a circuit. A useful experiment can still leave the household's hardest question unanswered.

headlineQuote: I like building a useful teaching sheet, but my partner Maya doesn't get paid because my apprentice understood a circuit.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, handling difficult faults and teaching apprentices.
He has **five months saved**, typical pay, some local firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren; Maya prepares supplier price offers.
He uses **AI daily**, tests early and keeps automated worksheet drafts inside employer, data, paid-time and instructor-check conditions.
Expected **partner income loss** alarms him in both faster AGI pictures, while extra years provide comparison time without inventing a replacement wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Maya's price-work income before replacement earnings, with later physical-work pressure around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and support with clear eligibility and costs would help.
Real practical learning needs **affordable fees** after essentials and no lost wages, rather than praise for enthusiasm.
